newsitem.title: USA: Judge says tobacco class-action likely to proceed.
newsitem.headline: Judge says tobacco class-action likely to proceed.

text.p: A Florida judge said Monday that tobacco company lawyers fighting a huge passive smoking lawsuit by flight attendants were unlikely to win separate trials for the hundreds of thousands of plaintiffs.

At a hearing before the start of the class-action lawsuit in June, the lawyers said lung cancer, heart ailments and other illnesses attributed by plaintiff's lawyers to secondhand smoke were too complex to lump in one trial.
"There is no way a jury can be asked to weed out these complications," said Hugh Whiting, an attorney for the R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings.

Whiting and lawyers for other tobacco companies such as Brown & Williamson, owned by B.A.T Industries Plc, said each case was different and the connection between a malady and secondhand smoke would have to individually proven.
Dade County Circuit Court Judge Robert Kaye said so many trials would be unwieldy and that he expected a two-part trial for the class-action suit brought by two Miami lawyers.

In the first, a jury will determine if cigarette makers conspired to keep evidence of the dangers of secondhand smoke from the public and whether the evidence was strong enough to link the illnesses of the flight attendants, who were non-smokers, to inhaling secondhand smoke while working.

A second trial will set monetary damages if the tobacco companies lose in the first. While Kaye stressed he had made no final decision, he said claims by the flight attendants could be grouped by category and be handled by one jury.
"There's no reason this trial cannot be tried by one jury," Kaye said.

The suit is one of several suits against the industry to come to trial in Florida and other states next year. Another Florida judge ruled on Friday that the state could sue cigarette makers under anti-racketeering laws, which could lead to triple damages against the tobacco companies.

At the hearing Monday, Kaye also said he was near a decision on how to reach the estimated 160,000 to 300,000 flight attendants who would be eligible for compensation if the industry lost the class-action suit.

Whiting pressed for a national media campaign, in addition to an agreed mailing to about 160,000 current and former flight attendants. He also proposed a toll-free telephone number, with costs to be borne by plaintiffs' lawyers.

Flight-attendants' attorneys Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt said such a campaign was wasteful and expensive and that word-of-mouth spurred by the mail campaign would lift the number of people joining the class-action.
